steps.title: Power cut: stay safe first
steps.detail: Unplug computers and other electronics so a power surge does not damage them when power returns. Use flashlights, not candles.
steps.why: Surges when power comes back can damage equipment. Candles are a fire risk.
steps.do_not: Never run a generator indoors or in a garage. It can kill with carbon monoxide.

steps.title: Check it is not an attack
steps.detail: Look for signs of an attack: a ransom message, files with strange names, accounts you cannot sign in to, money moved. If you see any, go back and choose that plan.
steps.why: An attack needs different steps than a normal outage, and the first minutes matter.

steps.title: Find out what is down and for whom
steps.detail: Check if other devices, other rooms or neighbors are affected. Note what does not work: internet, power, email, phones, card reader, a key system.
steps.why: Knowing the size of the problem tells you who to call: your provider, the utility or your IT contact.

steps.title: Call the provider and get a ticket number
steps.detail: Call your internet, phone or power provider from a mobile phone. Ask how long it should last and write down the ticket number.
steps.why: The ticket number speeds up follow-up calls and may be needed for a claim.

steps.title: Call your IT contact
steps.detail: Tell them what is down, since when, and what the provider said.
steps.why: They can check your own equipment and help you work around the problem.

steps.title: Switch to your backup way of working
steps.detail: Use a phone hotspot for urgent tasks, paper forms for orders or patients, and your card reader's offline mode if it has one. Keep a list of what you will need to enter later.
steps.why: Keeping the business running matters more than waiting for systems to come back.

steps.title: Tell staff and customers
steps.detail: Tell staff what still works and what to do instead. Put a short sign at the door or the counter if customers are affected.
steps.why: Clear, calm information avoids mistakes and frustration.

steps.title: Keep a simple timeline
steps.detail: Write down when it started, who you called, ticket numbers and what you did.
steps.why: It helps with follow-up calls, claims and planning for next time.

steps.title: When it comes back, restart step by step
steps.detail: Plug devices back in one at a time. Check that key systems and recent data are there. Enter the paper records.
steps.why: Restarting everything at once can trip power again, and checking data early finds problems while they are small.

steps.title: If you lost income or equipment, call your insurer
steps.detail: Tell them how long it lasted and what was damaged or lost. Give the ticket numbers.
steps.why: Some policies cover business interruption or damaged equipment.

steps.title: Afterwards, write down what would have helped
steps.detail: For example: a phone hotspot, a battery for the router, paper forms ready, a printed contacts card.
steps.why: Each outage shows what to prepare for the next one.

steps.title: If you think it was an attack outside the US, get help
steps.detail: In Canada, report it to the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security at cyber.gc.ca. In France, get help at cybermalveillance.gouv.fr. In the US, use the plan for that attack.
steps.why: National services can help you check and report an attack.
